author: 0xWast3
prompt: Opus 5.5 turned one sentence into a 3D system that opens in Blender, rigged, textured and ready to animate. It does not render the object. It constructs it, part by part, the way a modeller would if they had a week. > PARSE - the sentence becomes a parts list with real dimensions, nothing implied > MASS - each part built as clean geometry, quads only, no sculpted mush > RIG - joints and pivots placed where the object physically bends > SKIN - materials assigned per surface, scale and roughness set separately > PACK - exported with a named hierarchy, so a human can edit one part Image models stop at the render. What you get is a photograph of a thing that does not exist as a thing. That gap appears the second someone wants to move an arm, swap a material, or send it to a printer. author: yankis0x
prompt: The trick is NOT the prompt. It is one rule: every frame is a pure function of time. song -> numpy beat grid -> Opus 5.5 writes one HTML file -> Playwright renders -> ffmpeg blends step 1 -> pick a royalty-free track around 120 BPM step 2 -> give Opus 5.5 8 to 12 UI states: button, loader, toggle, chart, command palette step 3 -> one HTML file, 1440x1440, every style computed inside seek(t). no CSS transitions, no timers step 4 -> springs as closed-form math, so any frame renders in any order step 5 -> numpy finds the beats, every UI sound lands on a measured peak step 6 -> Playwright shoots 4 subframes per frame, ffmpeg tmix blends them into 60fps motion blur step 7 -> render one frame per beat first, fix what is off the grid, then the full render the math: 120 BPM x 7 bars = 28 beats = 14 seconds 14 s x 60 fps x 4 subframes = 3,360 browser renders
